cultivar: Mainly small- and medium-leaf types: Meitan, Shiqian and Guiding Niaowang local varieties, Fuding Dabai
processing: Ordinary green tea processing with the enzymes fixed by heat, then shaped and dried. The appellation includes several leaf shapes, among them curled and flat.
harvest_season: Picked from a single bud up to one bud with three leaves; as with other Chinese greens, the early spring picking is the most prized.
appearance_dry: Depends on style; the curled type is fine and tightly curled, downy and glossy green.
appearance_liquor: Bright yellow-green in the curled style.
appearance_wet: Tender, even, bright and lively leaf, largely whole.
taste_profile: Described as fresh and brisk with a full, rounded body and a high aroma; the exact character shifts with county, shape and picking grade.

brewing.notes: General guidance for Chinese greens: go cooler and shorter for bud-grade tea, and a little hotter for lots with more leaf.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's harvest, with spring lots leading and best drunk within about a year. It is an umbrella name, so the county and picking grade on the pack matter, and many teas are sold under their own local names as well.
description:
Guizhou Green Tea is a province-wide protected name, not a single recipe. It covers tea grown across 61 counties and districts of all nine of Guizhou's prefecture-level divisions, so think of it as a label of origin on a large and varied family of greens.

The registered rules allow picking from a lone bud up to one bud with three leaves, and they cover different shapes, among them curled and flat. That span explains why one Guizhou green can be delicate and downy while another is sturdier and cheaper.

The registered description is fresh, brisk and fairly full in the mouth, with a bright liquor. Brew it by the grade in front of you: bud-heavy tea wants water around 80 to 85°C and gentle steeps, while leafier tea can take more heat.

When buying, look for the county, the shape and the picking standard, since the umbrella name alone says little. Meitan, Duyun and Fenggang all have reputations of their own. Trying one tea from each is a good way to learn how wide the province is.
history:
Guizhou has a long record of tea, but this name as a formal appellation is recent. The national agriculture ministry registered it as an agricultural geographical indication on 10 January 2017, and the provincial government named it a lead brand for the province's tea that same year.

On 27 July 2020 it joined the second batch of names on the protection list under the China and EU geographical indications agreement. The registered production area is about 7 million mu of tea.
